did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with the heading “A Maskil of Asaph” and a painful question: “Why, O God, have you rejected us forever?” The image “the sheep of your pasture” presents Israel as a people under God’s protection.
The poet asks God to remember his people, Zion, and “the tribe of your inheritance.” Here, remembrance is connected both with past redemption and with the community’s present distress.

Verses 3–8 describe the desecration of the sanctuary, but they do not identify the enemy or give a date. The enemy is portrayed as raising cutting tools against the decorations of the place and then setting fire to the sanctuary and the sacred sites.

The enemies are described as roaring “in the midst of your meeting place” and even setting up their own signs where the sacred signs once stood. This emphasizes not only damage to the building, but also a hostile takeover of the place of worship.

The lament expresses a loss of guidance: “We do not see our signs,” “there is no longer a prophet,” and no one can say “How long?” The question is not only when the trouble will end, but also how it can be understood.

Despite the feeling that God is hidden, the poet declares: “Yet God is my King from long ago.” Remembering God as King and as the one who performs acts of salvation provides the basis for asking him to act again now.

The poet recalls God’s rule over the sea and the sea creatures: he “broke the heads of the monsters” and crushed “the heads of Leviathan.” The passage also goes on to mention springs, rivers, and waters.

God’s rule is also described as cosmic order: day and night, the heavenly light and the sun, the boundaries of the earth, summer and winter. In this way, the psalm moves from describing destruction to recognizing the order of creation.

The poet asks God to look upon the covenant, because the land is full of “the dark places of the earth” and “the haunts of violence.” Alongside this request, he explicitly mentions the poor and needy and asks that they not return in disgrace.

At the end, God is called upon to “Arise” and plead his own cause. The psalm concludes by asking him to remember the enemy’s disgrace and uproar, so the protection of the people is presented also as protection of his name and honor.
